## English translation

#### Robin Hood: The Legend of Sherwood

- Review score (out of 10): **8**
- Text / voices: Spanish · Genre: Strategy · Developer: Spellbound Entertainment Software · Release: 27/11/2002 · Platform: PC

#### The one in the hood

The indefatigable hero of the goatee, bow, and hood arrives on our computer in this good tactical-combat game from Spellbound—yes, the same people who developed *Desperados*, very much inspired by the successful Spanish game *Commandos*.

**The legendary Robin Hood, brought to the cinema so many times, is the protagonist of this game clearly inspired by *Commandos*. The friend of the poor, the green-clad hooded rogue, has returned to the PC to fight the Sheriff accompanied by his friends. This famous hero has rarely been brought to videogames, but judging by the quality of the games in which Robin Hood was the protagonist, it has been done with considerable success (someone please explain who translated “hood” as “forest”).**

Like *Commandos*, this is a tactical-combat game in which missions must be carried out by using each character’s abilities. Although it is inspired by the magnificent Spanish game, it has different aspects which, together with its medieval setting, make it genuinely interesting.

In fact, I think the only serious criticism one can make is that it resembles *Commandos* too much. It is nevertheless a very entertaining game that makes us think and keeps us occupied. On top of that, it is translated and dubbed into Spanish, something that can be considered exceptional.

If you liked *Commandos* 1 and 2 and *Desperados* too, you will like *Robin Hood* as long as you are not tired of this kind of game—which cannot exactly be called common either. But first I recommend that you read this review, in which I will try to make very clear what you will find when you install it on your computer.

#### Audio and video

*Robin Hood* is a two-dimensional game in an isometric (or pseudo-isometric; in reality it is not isometric) perspective, the usual one in games of this style. Being 2D allows it to have richly detailed and generally very high-quality settings, something much more difficult to achieve in a 3D game. The game’s greatest graphical quality lies precisely in how carefully its settings have been made: medieval cities represented in complete detail and leafy forests in which to hide our dear outlaws.

The cities, villages, and castles contain numerous stone houses with wooden roofs where one can distinguish every joint separating the stones or the boards forming the roof. On the trees, the roughness of the bark and the moss or lichens clinging to it can be distinguished. It is very detailed work, and the great effort of the graphic artists in designing the settings must be acknowledged. Of course, there are not very many settings either; to some extent, it is only natural that they worked on them so much.

Another aspect of the settings is the water found in streams or castle moats, where an excellent job can be seen. The water has reflections and movement, and the small cascades running over the rocks are especially well done. Do not forget that these are 2D graphics.

The characters, by contrast, do not measure up. They are too small, and even more so if we increase the screen resolution. There are large icons showing their faces in greater detail, which is appreciated because otherwise we would be unable to make out their features. You can zoom in, but it is the typical 2D zoom that enlarges the pixels too, like the one in *Commandos*, reducing the graphical quality.

You can enter buildings. In some cases the character remains inside or comes out through another door without us seeing the interior; on other occasions, depending on the building, we can see inside because the exterior part that would block our view disappears. The interior has the same level of detail as the exterior.

The game’s atmosphere is also very good. There is day and night, which is when we can appreciate how well the lighting has been made, with shadows and everything—although, naturally, they are not dynamic shadows. That would be too much for a 2D game.

The bad thing is that the characters often remain hidden behind a building and we cannot see what is happening. We can still control them, but if they are in combat we cannot watch it. This would be solved by being able to change the viewpoint as in *Commandos 2*, but that aspect was not copied.

The sound is nothing wonderful, but as an almost exceptional piece of news I will say that it is dubbed into Spanish. Yes, believe it or not, a game dubbed into Spanish. The text is translated too, of course. The bad thing about the dubbing is the usual thing: it sounds like a cartoon. Even so, I am not going to criticize this aspect. The one time a game with Spanish dubbing appears, the best thing is simply to applaud it.

I said that the sound is nothing wonderful, but it fulfils its job of creating atmosphere. In fact, a little more ambient sound is missing, but it is not too important—at least not to me. The voices have a certain charm, especially for younger players, with combat phrases such as “night-night” when the big fellow hits an enemy on the head with his club.

The music is good, very well suited to the period, and does not become too repetitive... but I turn it off. I usually do that in almost every game, except for a few.

If you are looking for a game with good 2D graphics, you will certainly find them in this *Robin Hood*. Apart from the detail of the characters, the graphics pass with good marks; this section would score even higher with a little more ambient sound.

#### Story

Well, surely more or less everyone knows the story of Robin Hood, a legendary hero whom many consider a real one. Even if only because of the many films made about Robin with the Goatee, his story will sound familiar. This game is based on that story and unfolds as tactical missions integrated into the plot. The plot does not have a huge presence in the game, but it does make it more appealing, so I will tell you a little about it in case anyone no longer remembers this character.

The story of Robin Hood takes place in twelfth-century medieval England, one of the darkest periods of this age. King Richard the Lionheart is away on the Crusades liberating Jerusalem, while in England Prince John Lackland rules like Aznar, roughing up the peasants and sucking away their money through taxes.

After a long absence caused by the Crusades, Robin of Locksley returns to England and finds this situation: the peasants are being cruelly exploited, and he also discovers that his father has died and that, since Robin was presumed dead, his lands have been expropriated by the Sheriff of Nottingham.

So imagine how our rogue friend feels. In desperation he goes to ask his friend Sir Godwin of Lincoln for help, to find out what happened while he was away, but the castle is occupied by soldiers and Sir Lincoln has disappeared.

Without money or shelter, Robin wanders around and comes across a group of peasants who are about to be executed. He helps them escape, and they take refuge in Sherwood Forest, where they establish a camp and decide to become outlaws and rogues in order to defend their freedom. The grateful peasants make Robin their leader, and from then on they will rob priests and nobles and distribute their riches among the peasants. They become very popular, getting many people to join them and form a band of outlaws who ambush Prince John’s tax collectors.

But when Lady Marian, the protagonist’s girl, tells him that King Richard has been imprisoned and that Prince John plans not to pay the ransom to free him, Robin begins organizing a rebellion against the prince. And that is how the legend of Robin Hood is forged, one who would have a daughter called Little Red Riding Hood who walked through the forest... but that is another story.

That is the plot, and the game unfolds through missions related to the story: missions to rescue peasants or friends detained by the Sheriff, ambushes of tax collectors, robberies... and always setting out from the camp in Sherwood, where we can train peasants or build equipment for the missions.

There are not many ways to play: simply follow the story in single-player and nothing more. There is no cooperative multiplayer, one of *Commandos*’ best options, nor is there a tutorial.

In the game you can control several unique characters, such as Robin Hood himself, Little John, Lady Marian, the drunken monk Tuck, Will Scarlett, and Stutely, Robin’s old friend. Each has their own abilities, but there are also characters who will join the group. They have different abilities but are not unique; in other words, they can be repeated, although their names change. We can have four or more strongmen or a good number of identical rogues with different names.

#### Gameplay

This is a tactical-combat game very much in the style of *Commandos*, but with some differences. The main one is that instead of progressing mission by mission and thereby seeing new maps, here there are a few settings that we must visit several times for different missions, always setting out from our camp in Sherwood.

Another important difference is that we manage some resources. If we want to shoot arrows, we have to make them, and if we want a net with which to entangle the enemy, we have to make those too. Items are manufactured in the camp by putting characters to work in the appropriate workshop; when we return from the mission, we can see the result. The number of workers we have determines how quickly we make the items.

Characters gain experience as they enter combat, or when we put them through training in the camp. They become better the more we use them, which means we must take special care that none of them is killed. They also improve their abilities, of which there are many and each is more useful than the last. In combat we will also notice that they are very different from *Commandos*, since we can choose the blows the characters will deliver or tell them when to take cover.

Orders are given by pressing the mouse and moving it around the enemy, making an 8, an ellipse, or curved or straight lines. Each character has their own range of blows, with different effects on the opponent.

Otherwise, it plays in a way very similar to *Commandos*. We choose the group we want to take on the mission at the camp, then control them there to complete it by using their abilities, crouching, bonking people, or climbing walls. There are many ways to finish missions, as well as the familiar system showing where guards are looking and the reach of their vision.

The missions are very entertaining and offer plenty of possibilities. If they seem too easy, we can change the difficulty level, which is advisable because the enemies are quite stupid and easy. The fact that the enemies are so foolish is worth criticizing. Often this detracts somewhat from the rest of the game. During missions we may also encounter an extra task, generally involving helping peasants, which in turn will provide us with items, money, or more recruits for our camp.

*Robin Hood* is very easy to control, but this ease has nothing to do with the difficulty the missions may have. The missions are also very varied and entertaining, with several ways to complete them successfully. A good game that will give us many enjoyable moments.

#### Strategy and tips

In this kind of game, the main thing is to stop and think about every move and do things in advance. These are games of tactics and of making use of the characters’ characteristics. The main advice is to try not to kill enemies: simply knock them unconscious and then tie them up, leaving them in places away from patrols so the patrols do not see and untie them. Not killing them means greater popularity among the peasants and a greater number of volunteers joining our cause. It is a little unrealistic; I imagine that in the Middle Ages the thing that would generate the most popularity would be killing the person who is bombarding you with taxes, but this is a game, not reality.

Clearly, you must avoid being discovered. To do this, characters can crouch to make themselves harder to detect. Always use the icon that shows the guards’ cone of vision; it lets you know where they are really looking and how far they can see. This range is also reduced at night or in fog.

All characters have special abilities. Some can throw an apple to distract someone temporarily, pick locks, release nets, whistle, disguise themselves as a beggar, let another character climb onto their shoulders, and many other things. You must take advantage of all of them according to the situation; very often using an ability will be indispensable to finish a mission.

But the most important thing for getting through missions is to use a couple of strongmen, characters like Little John who carry a mace and knock enemies unconscious three at a time in combat. He alone can practically take out all the guards as long as there are not too many archers. Afterwards, all you have to do is tie up the bodies left lying on the ground. The truth is that a strongman helps a lot in missions.

To have items at the start of missions, the peasants who are not in the group must stay behind working and making things, so that new items are ready when we return from the mission.

#### Compared with...

Can’t you guess?... let’s see... no, not *Flight Simulator*! *Commandos* 1 or 2. Good grief... Since this game was clearly inspired by *Commandos*, it is normal to compare it with that Spanish game. First it loses out in one respect: innovation. *Commandos* was innovative, the second one less so, and this one even less. That already puts it at a disadvantage, because it is always more commendable to make something attractive and novel.

In graphics, *Commandos 2* also wins, as it does in the number of settings, and our *Commandos* is better in camera options too. In addition, *Robin Hood* has no cooperative multiplayer, while *Commandos* lets us play with our friends, each controlling a character. *Commandos* is also better in character abilities, but what I like more about this game is going to the camp to organize resources and have the characters gain experience.

I think *Commandos* is a much better game, but this one is not bad at all. It is on *Desperados*’ level—better in some things and worse in others, but at that level. Now it will depend on how you value the fact that it resembles *Commandos* too much, something that can be considered a source of pride since *Commandos* is Spanish, and it is always nice for others to imitate us rather than the reverse happening.

#### What is good

That it resembles *Commandos*; the characters’ abilities; the graphics; resource management; the ability to gain experience; and the atmosphere in the cities. Naturally, the fact that it is dubbed and translated is positive.

#### What is not so good

That it resembles *Commandos*; it has no multiplayer; the artificial intelligence is very artificial; and the characters are too small.

#### Manual and translation

The game is completely translated and dubbed into Spanish, so it is understandable that the manual is too. It is 21 pages explaining how to play and the different options. It does not need to be any longer, since one learns to play quickly even without a manual.

The translation is good and I did not find any important errors. The text is not extremely long either, but it is something, and it is well translated. The game comes on a CD in a DVD case and takes one gigabyte of hard-drive space to install.

#### Links

[Official website](http://www.robinhood-game.com) · [Fine Weitere fan page](http://mitglied.lycos.de/robinhoodgame/robinhood/)

#### Required equipment

This is not a game that requires many resources, and I think it can run well on a PIII 450, 128 MB of RAM, and a DirectX-compatible video card.

I tested it on a PIII 1000, 512 MB of RAM, and a GeForce 2. Obviously, it runs perfectly with all details at maximum.

**Review score (out of 10): 8**

### Very good

A well-finished game that we will enjoy and remember. A good purchase, highly recommended for fans of the genre. It is carefully made at every level. **Buy it.**
